newsitem.title: MEXICO: Latin American pension reforms no goldmine yet.
newsitem.headline: Latin American pension reforms no goldmine yet.

text.p: Latin America is carving up a slew of bankrupt and often corrupt state pension systems, but analysts say it may take years before the reforms provide a mine of new wealth as they have in pioneering Chile.

Chile's pension reform, replacing an almost insolvent pay-as-you-go state scheme with mandatory private pensions, was launched in 1980 by a former military dictatorship intent on curbing the state's role in the economy.
Its success, more than a decade later, has prompted envious and cash-hungry neighbors to follow suit.

But democracy has turned out to be a fickle friend of reform, and in some cases more accountable governments have found it difficult to exit the pension business, because of political pressure and union opposition.

That, analysts say, may undermine its future growth potential. The four countries following Chile in introducing private pension systems -- Peru (1992), Argentina (1994), Colombia (1994) and Uruguay (1996) -- have kept a state-run option, and private affiliation started slowly.

Mexico and Bolivia plan to introduce private pensions shortly but Mexico has retained a pension management firm run by the state Social Security Institute, and that is expected to muscle in heavily on the new system.
"The speed with which contributors move from a public to a private system is influenced by politics," said Jose Garcia-Cantera, bank analyst at Salomon Brothers in New York.
"In Chile in 1981 there was a political system that resulted in everybody being forced to go into the new private system very quickly."

That, he says, partly explains the exponential growth of assets under management by pension funds in Chile, which currently account for 40 percent of gross domestic product, or around $30 billion, after just 15 years.

In a recent report, Salomon Brothers projected the estimated amount of assets under management in Latin America by the year 2011. Its estimates, that it stressed were conservative, ranged from 14.7 percent for Uruguay to 23.4 percent in Colombia.
Chile's, by contrast, were expected to surge to 67 percent. Its fast growth to date has been largely fueled by returns on assets that averaged 12.5 percent since 1981.
Salomon Brothers estimated, again conservatively, that the real returns for Latin American pension funds over the next 15 years may average as little as three percent.

But the investment bank is upbeat on the implications of private pension funds as a whole, saying they would strengthen domestic savings, and help develop capital markets in a region that lacks long-term investment instruments.

Mexico's reform, it added, was likely to be particularly dynamic because it allows pension fund administrators to manage multiple funds and puts no limit on investments -- two features other countries including Chile do not enjoy.
President Ernesto Zedillo has touted Mexico's system as the key to boosting the country's lackluster savings rate but analysts say it also has its drawbacks may not be the panacea Zedillo predicts.

"It's not clear to me that the Mexican design is in any way superior to the Chilean one, even though Chile's has a number of flaws," said Sebastian Edwards, a former World Bank chief economist and now a professor at UCLA in Los Angeles.

He said the powerful role that the social security institute will continue to play running its own pension fund in competition with private Afores, as the funds are known in Mexico, was "a matter of great concern".

Zedillo's decision to delay the planned launch of the Afores from January 1997 to September -- citing a need to simplify the worker registration system -- also set off alarm bells. Edwards said he would not be surprised if it was put back further because of its high fiscal costs.

"The delay sends a bad signal. Zedillo has made it the core of his term in office. The six-year economic plan put up by the Zedillo administration calls for a tremendous increase in national savings," he told Reuters.

How soon pension funds boost domestic savings is also unclear. Edwards pointed out that while the state retains responsibility for paying existing retirees, contributions are simply shifted from the public to the private sector, meaning no net gain until they start generating compounded returns.
"How soon that starts to happen we don't know. Maybe five to eight years," he said.
Another wholly innovative system that was due to be launched early this year is Bolivia's, blending privatization with the creation of a mandatory private pension fund system.
Under the new scheme, the government will sell 50 percent of some large state-owned companies, but the money paid by investors will go directly toward capitalizing the firm.
The other 50 percent will be fully transferred to the Bolivian population into trust funds eventually to be managed by the pension funds.
The reform, approved by Congress in November, met with howls of protest from trade unions and health workers, however. The Catholic Church damned it as "individualist".
The odd one out in the region, neighboring Brazil, has not yet introduced a private pension fund system, and many proposed reforms have been stubbornly blocked in Congress.
But as of mid-1996, the country already had some $66 billion of assets managed by 350 closed pension funds owned by private and state corporations -- a unique feature in Latin America.
Salomon Brothers said the amount managed by Brazil's pension funds could reach at least $241 billion by 2011.
